title: A Very Long Time
mood: The night the base fell, Chang’e writes a letter she never sends. Across the water, Lesley keeps watch for years.

hero.alt: Close on Chang'e's green eyes behind her round glasses, tears running down, embers drifting past.

segs.t: On Chang’e’s screen the cursor still blinked after
Lesley, the coil runs cooler now.
Above it the log ran back for years, every entry to the same name. Far up was one she never scrolled back to. She did not need to.
The research base. The night it fell.
The lab was cold. Its door stood open, the way she had left it when they ran.
The researcher who had given her the big bench carried her in from the yard. He set her down inside the door and put his own coat round her. It smelled of the storehouse fire.
“The shelter’s this way,” he said. “Come on.”
“No.”
Someone shouted for him down the corridor. He looked at her, then down the corridor, and went.
The red lamps had died with the alarm. Only the console still glowed.
At the back of the lab the frame stood where it always stood, beside the test ring. In the console’s glow she could read the page still pinned to its foot.
For whoever has to stand in front.
Under it, in her mother’s quick hand:
First light.
One corner of the page had curled. Chang’e pressed it flat.
Mr. Bunny lay dark on the bench beside the photograph, his casing open.
Leave him,
her father had said.
She shut the casing. It clicked. She switched him on.
He rose and swung around to the front, where she could see his face. It was the face she had made for Sis’s homecoming. One round eye, one teal one. The teal one winked.
It was still too slow.
She wiped it away. His own face came back.
She laid the photograph face down.
Under the bench the cold box hummed. At its front stood the fourth cup, SIS across its lid in her own pencil. She pushed it to the back, behind everything, where nobody would see it.
Then she climbed into her father’s chair at the console. Her feet hung off the floor.
The log opened where she had left it.
Lesley, it held! You missed it. Come home.
That evening they had lifted her up between them, and her mother had laughed.
She promised,
thought Chang’e.
She started a new line under it.
I’ll never forgive you, Lesley. You were not here when we needed your protection. They died because of you!
She read it twice. Her fingers began another line on their own.
I had my eyes
They stopped. She deleted it one letter at a time.
She did not send the entry. She saved it under the other one and closed the file.

Beside her, Mr. Bunny’s face went away. He had turned to the window, and his lens showed what it saw. A far rooftop up the shore stood black against the red sky. On it sat a small figure, a long rifle across its knees, looking at the lab.
Chang’e did not look up. “Turn around,” she said.
He turned his lens back to the console.
The next night his lens drifted to the window again, and the figure was on his screen.
“Turn around.”
And the night after that.
The years after.
On the third night the same researcher came with soup. Yesterday’s bowl stood by the console, full, with a skin on it.
He swapped them. “There’s a home in the city. For children who...” He did not finish. “They have beds. Someone cooks.”
“Who would finish it?” asked Chang’e.
“Finish what?”
She pointed at the frame without turning around.
He looked at the frame. “It won’t bring them back.”
“I won’t forgive anyone who tries to destroy the world,” said Chang’e.
He took the old bowl and went. He never said “home” again. After that two of the others came with him, with bread and blankets, and carried away what she had not eaten.
Her mother’s notebook lay beside the console, open at the last page. Someone had brought it over from the bench.
First light. Held past three hundred, no shaking. C.’s hand on the plate. Next:
The line stopped there.
Chang’e picked up the pencil. Under
Next:
, in letters twice the size of her mother’s, she wrote:
Make it something a soldier can wear.
Then she opened the suit’s file and worked until the windows went gray.
At midnight nobody said “Bed.”
A week after the fall, Lesley got the Shield to post two soldiers she trusted on the base’s gate.
“What are we guarding?” one asked.
“The base.”
“And if the girl asks who sent us?”
“The Shield sent you.”
Months later the officer with gray in his beard brought her an armband. It made her a commander of the Shield’s combat division.
“The squads asked for you,” he said. “You held the avenues.”
I held the wrong place,
thought Lesley. She put the armband on.
Before her first raid in command, a boy at the end of the line asked what they did if the Enders ran.
Lesley worked her rifle’s bolt and let it slide home.
“Not a single enemy will escape.”
She asked the Shield for one thing for herself: a room at the top of an old tower across the water.
“It’s cold up there,” said the quartermaster. “Nobody wants it.”
“It has a window.”
The window faced the lab’s. She carried up one hard chair and set it facing the glass, with its back to the door.
That first night she found the lit window in her sights.
The small figure was at the console, asleep. Her cheek lay on the desk. A pencil was still in her fingers.
Once Lesley would have taken it out of her hand and carried her to bed.
Think in bed,
she thought.
At her collar the comm was on the base’s channel. It hissed. Her thumb found the call switch and rested there.
Let her sleep.
She did not press it. Nobody called her either.
She was still watching when the first boats went out on the water.
In the second year Chang’e sealed a core for the next suit inside a glass chamber. A copper plate was set into its wall. She laid her palm on the plate, and the core lit.
Then she pumped out the air.
The hum died, and one by one the needles fell to nothing. The light held.
She wrote down what she had seen. She did not know yet what the finding was good for. In the margin she added her mother’s words:
A guess is not a claim.
By the third year, finished suits stood beside the old frame. Their gray plates were bolted over steel.
The Shield sent soldiers to try them. None of them could make a suit so much as lift its arm.
Terrinia had suits now, and still nothing that could beat the Enders.
The city’s scientists came to see them. The oldest of them read her report and stopped at one line.
Chang’e had crossed out
belief
there. Above it she had written
aspirant power
He looked at her over the page. “You crossed out belief.”
“Belief sits still,” said Chang’e. “This reaches.”
An aspirant was a person reaching for something with everything in them. That was what lit a core.
He copied the word into his own report.

That week the scientists made her Chief Scientist, the youngest Terrinia had ever had. It had been her parents’ title. The old plate on the lab door had said CHIEF SCIENTISTS. The new one was the same, without the last S.
She stood in the doorway under it until Mr. Bunny came around to the front.
On a clean page she began a new design. At the top, where her mother had always written who a project was for, she wrote:
OBJECTIVE: KEEP HERSELF SAFE
So nobody has to push me clear again,
she thought. She did not write that part.
She built it in the test ring at the back of the lab, where the robot arms could hold the pieces while she welded. The pieces were crescents, white edged with pink.
At the first test they rose a hand’s width and dropped. They clattered across the floor. Mr. Bunny’s screen winced.
“Again,” said Chang’e.
Weeks later she carried the crescents into the yard at night. She sat down cross-legged among them at the crater’s edge, and a ring of light woke around her.
“Aspirant power, guide me,” said Chang’e.
The crescents lifted. They circled her once, slowly, then faster, until the yard shone white and pink.

media.alt: Seen from behind, small Chang'e climbs a long stair alone; a white crescent edged with pink hangs in the robot arm of a steel test ring; then her gloved hands spread and she sits in a ring of light among the crescents.

segs.t: Back at the console she opened the log.
Lesley, I have finally developed my new weapon. With it, I can protect others now.
Her finger stopped over the send key. Then she saved it with the rest.
Across the water, Lesley had watched the yard light up.
Her eye drew the crescents in thin teal lines as they circled the small figure. She had never seen a weapon like it. It guarded the one inside it and needed nobody else.
After that the raids thinned. Then, for a long time, nothing came at all.
By then Lesley and Chang’e had not spoken in a very long time.
She slept in the hard chair, facing the window. The dream came as it always did, and ended on the same voice.
“Go away! Leave me alone!”
Lesley woke.
The cries and screams went on.

media.alt: Lesley, seen from behind with her long gold hair over her face, lifts a gloved hand to her visor; beyond her the city lies dark under drifting embers.

segs.t: Her hand went to the visor, the way it always did after the dream. It stopped there. Out in the dark, fires were going up across the city, and the sirens had started.
This was no dream. The Enders had finally come back.
That stubborn girl will go out alone,
she thought.
Like I did.
She stood up with the rifle in her hand.
Not this time.
